s1.quote: She lies in 8 to 9 metres of murky water on a muddy seabed. … visible at all states of the tide

s2.quote: Area: Sand bank between Greenock and Helensburgh … her thinner deck plates are starting to rust through with holes opening up in places.

hazards.text: Murky, silty water on a muddy seabed
Deck plates rusting through, holes opening up

summary.text: A sugar freighter that grounded on a sandbank in the middle of the Clyde between Greenock and Helensburgh, still partly above water at every tide. Below, the hull sits in murky, silty water around 9 m and is deteriorating.

s1.quote: ran aground on the Doom Bar as the tide was ebbing … sand completely covers the site, preventing further investigation at this time.

notDiveSite.reason: Wreck is off Padstow (Doom Bar), Cornwall, not the Firth of Forth; sand covers the site and it has not been located

s1.quote: The submarine was finally salvaged on 15 March, repaired and recommissioned as HMS K22.

notDiveSite.reason: Raised in 1917, recommissioned as K22 and later scrapped; no wreck on the Gareloch seabed

s1.quote: Her last voyage was on 20 June 1936, and she was broken up at Bo'ness, Scotland.

notDiveSite.reason: Scrapped at Bo'ness in 1936; no wreck

s1.quote: has never been found, not least because 500 other shipwrecks lie at the bottom of the Firth of Forth.

sites.name: HMS Campania

s1.quote: The wreck site lies at a depth of 22-25m below chart datum, 1.7km SSE of the entrance to Burntisland harbour, Fife. … Responsible recreational diving is encouraged.

s3.quote: This designation was revoked in 2013 when the site was re-designated as a Historic Marine Protected Area.

access.value: Historic Marine Protected Area: responsible diving encouraged, no artefact recovery, file a visit report with HES

summary.text: The remains of a Cunard liner turned seaplane carrier lie off Burntisland in the Firth of Forth, in roughly 22-25 m. A protected site, it is still a big upstanding iron hull that divers may visit under HES guidelines.

sites.depthNote: Seabed 22-25 m; hull stands up to ~12 m proud

notDiveSite.reason: A 65 km sea loch, not a single dive site

s1.quote: She now lies off Yellowcraigs beach in 6m of water … Seabed depths are around 6.5 – 7 metres at high water and 3-4 metres at low water. … mostly buried in the sand.

s2.quote: although well broken up, her remains are still visible just above the surface at low tide.

hazards.text: Wreck mostly buried; structures stand 3-4 m off seabed

summary.text: A broken-up former US destroyer (later HMS Ludlow) used as a rocket target, lying off Yellowcraigs beach in about 6 m. Much is buried in sand in two sections, with remains breaking the surface at low tide.

sites.name: HMS Pathfinder

s1.quote: in 62 metres of water and rises 8 metres above the seabed … there is ammunition scattered among the wreckage … To date the wreck has not been officially protected

s2.quote: which lies 68m (223ft) below the surface … The wreck is in remarkably good condition.

summary.text: The WWI cruiser torpedoed by U-21 lies upright off St Abbs Head, roughly 62-68 m down, and is reported in remarkably good condition. Only suited to technical divers; she is a war grave.

sites.depthNote: Seabed 62 m (one source says 68 m); wreck rises ~8 m

s1.quote: The least depth over the wreck is around 43-44 metres dependant on the state of the tide. … lie in position 56°07.295’N, 02°46.464’W in 54 metres … The extensive wreckage is still fairly in tact with her distinctive sloping bow
The site of the two sunken submarines, 100 metres apart and about 50 metres down

s2.quote: The site of the two sunken submarines, 100 metres apart and about 50 metres down, has long been known.

s3.quote: The wreck is designated as a protected place under the Protection of Military Remains Act 1986.

access.value: Protected place under the Protection of Military Remains Act 1986 (war grave)

s1.quote: The dispersed remains of the cruiser HMS Argyll lie in 6m depth of water to the W of the Bell Rock. … The guns and propellers have been removed.

summary.text: Scattered remains of a cruiser that ran onto the Bell Rock reef in 1915, lying in about 6 m just west of the lighthouse. Her guns and propellers were salvaged, but she is still regarded as diveable.
